dialect: Intel 8086, 16-bit real mode, written for the NASM assembler (the dialect of the retro game)

size.label: instructions in the original 8086 list
size.detail: The list puts some families on one line, for example all conditional jumps.

size.label: written forms of those instructions
size.detail: This count includes each conditional jump and its synonyms, for example JE and JZ.
size.source: Counted from the same Wikipedia table

size.label: register names
size.detail: 8 general registers, 4 segment registers, IP and FLAGS.

size.label: instruction names in modern x86-64
size.detail: Each new processor generation added words. We do not need them for the game.

words.meaning: Copy a value from one place to a different place.
Swap the values in two places.
Put a value on the top of the stack.
Take the value from the top of the stack.
Calculate an address and keep the address. It does not read the memory.
Register A, the primary work register (16 bits). AH and AL are its two halves.
Register B. It often holds a memory address.
Register C, the counter. LOOP and REP count down with it.
Register D. It holds the high half of large results, and port numbers.
Source index. It points to the place where data comes from.
Destination index. It points to the place where data goes.
Base pointer. It points into the stack.
Stack pointer. It points to the top of the stack.
Data segment. It selects the 64 KB area that holds the data.
Extra segment. It selects a second area, for example the screen memory.
Code segment. It selects the area that holds the instructions.
Stack segment. It selects the area that holds the stack.
A pile of values in memory. The last value in is the first value out.
Square brackets mean "the value at this address", not the address.
Size: 8 bits, one value from 0 to 255.
Size: 16 bits, one value from 0 to 65,535.
Define bytes. Put these bytes in the program file.
Define words. Put these 16-bit numbers in the program file.
Reserve bytes. Keep this much empty space.
Give a name to a number.
Table lookup: replace AL with the byte at [BX + AL]. One verb reads one entry of a table.
Add a value.
Subtract a value.
Add 1.
Subtract 1.
Multiply numbers that have no sign. The result goes in DX and AX.
Multiply numbers that have a sign.
Divide numbers that have no sign. AX gets the result, DX gets the remainder.
Divide numbers that have a sign.
Change the sign. 5 becomes -5.
Move the bits left. Each step multiplies by 2.
Move the bits right. Each step divides by 2 (numbers with no sign).
Move the bits right and keep the sign. Each step divides a signed number by 2.
Keep only the bits that are 1 in the two values.
Set each bit that is 1 in one value or the other.
Flip the bits where the two values differ. xor ax, ax sets AX to 0.
Flip every bit.
Add, plus the carry flag. It joins the high bytes of a number that is longer than one register.
Subtract, minus the carry flag (the borrow). The partner of ADC.
Decimal adjust after an ADD or ADC of two packed decimal bytes in AL. It makes 09h + 1 into 10h and sets CF after 99.
Decimal adjust after a SUB or SBB of two packed decimal bytes in AL. The partner of DAA.
Divide AL by 10. The tens go to AH, the units stay in AL: a ready-made step to show a number under 100.
Make a signed number longer: CBW copies the sign of AL into AH. CWD copies the sign of AX into DX, before IDIV.
Carry flag. It is 1 when a result is too large for its size.
Compare two values. It subtracts but keeps only the flags.
Compare the bits of two values. It does an AND but keeps only the flags.
Go to a label.
Go to a label if the compared values are equal (the zero flag is 1).
Go to a label if the compared values are not equal.
Go to a label if less / greater (numbers with a sign).
Go to a label if below / above (numbers with no sign).
Subtract 1 from CX. If CX is not 0, go to the label.
Go to a subroutine and remember the return address.
Return to the instruction after the CALL.
Zero flag. It is 1 when the last result is zero.
Sign flag. It is 1 when the last result is negative.
A name for a place in the program. A colon ends it.
Do the next string verb again, CX times.
Copy one byte from DS:SI to ES:DI, then move SI and DI to the next byte.
Copy one word (2 bytes) from DS:SI to ES:DI.
Put AL at ES:DI, then move DI to the next byte.
Put AX at ES:DI, then move DI 2 bytes.
Load the byte at DS:SI into AL, then move SI.
Make the string verbs move forward (clear the direction flag).
Direction flag. It sets the direction of the string verbs.
Tell the assembler the start address of the program. A DOS .COM program starts at 100h.
Select 16-bit or 32-bit translation.
Put the next lines in a named part of the file, for code or for data.
Give a name to a piece of text.
Give a name to a group of instructions. Then use the name as one word.
Read a different file at this point.
Do the rest of the line again, a number of times.
Put the bytes of a file into the program at this place. This is how the A side reads a table that the B side made.
Starts a comment. The assembler ignores the rest of the line.
Separates the destination (first) from the source (second).
At the end of a number, h marks base 16 (hexadecimal). 10h is 16.
Call a service of the BIOS or DOS (a ready-made routine in the computer).
DOS: show the text at DS:DX. A $ sign marks the end of the text.
DOS: show one character. The character is in DL.
DOS: stop the program and return to DOS.
BIOS: wait for a key. The BIOS puts the key code in AX.
BIOS: tell if a key is ready, without a wait.
BIOS: change the screen to 320 x 200 pixels with 256 colors (Mode 13h).
BIOS: change the screen to text mode again.
Read a value from a hardware port.
Write a value to a hardware port.
Stop hardware interrupts for a short time.
Let hardware interrupts start again.
Return from an interrupt handler.
Stop the processor until the next interrupt.
A numbered door to a hardware device. The processor talks to devices through ports.
A signal that stops the program for a moment, runs a handler, then lets the program continue.
The segment of the VGA screen memory in Mode 13h. Each byte is one pixel.
The VGA status port. Bit 3 is 1 while the screen beam returns to the top (vertical retrace).
The VGA palette ports. Select a color number, then write its red, green and blue parts.
The keyboard interrupt. A game replaces its handler to read keys fast.
